newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers move towards ending strike.
newsitem.headline: French truckers move towards ending strike.

text.p: Truck drivers were lifting roadblocks all over France on Friday after their unions signed a deal with employers on early retirement and reported substantial progress on pay and work-time claims to end a 12-day strike.

Truckers began voting with their wheels ahead of the weekend even before negotiations ended in Paris, lifting many of the blockades that have strangled the economy and forced petrol rationing in half the country.

By 5 p.m. (1600 GMT), two hours after talks ended at the Transport Ministry, the number of roadblocks had fallen to 180 from a peak of 249 on Thursday and an official at the national traffic information centre said they were "just melting away".
"Our feeling is that our profession has won dignity and recognition in these 12 days of struggle," said Claude Debons, spokesman for the biggest union, the Socialist-led CFDT.
Negotiators signed five agreements covering retirement at 55 instead of 60 for drivers with 25 years' service, sick pay, travel expenses, union rights and a ban on Sunday driving.

The employers doubled their offer of a special bonus payment to 3,000 francs ($600) and the government promised a decree on work time within two weeks meeting key demands for full payment for hours worked including unloading time and compulsory rest.
The unions said that would be equivalent to at least a 10 percent pay rise.

Embattled Prime Minister Alain Juppe ruled out using force to clear the roads and said on Thursday a settlement was urgent as "the consequences (of a prolonged strike) on our economy, on many companies, on many workers risk being very damaging".

While the end of the strike removed the risk of wider economic damage, political commentators said it had highlighted Juppe's weakness with both sides leaning on the government to sign cheques to settle the dispute.

The state made most of the concessions in the private sector dispute by agreeing to cut payroll taxes on employers and help finance early retirement for truckers. It also had to step in to resolve the working hours issue by decree.
Strikers lifted their blockade of the main Channel port of Calais, allowing stranded British and foreign trucks to board ferries, and on the Belgian, German and Italian borders.
Roadblocks around major oil refineries near Nantes, Nice and Strasbourg were lifted, and authorities reported trucks leaving the key Berre refineries near Marseille.

The Industry Ministry said up to 10,000 petrol stations -- more than half of the nation's 18,000 -- had run dry or were about to close and it would take two to three days for supplies to resume fully.

Unions voiced satisfaction with a draft decree which they said went a long way towards meeting their thorniest demand -- the abolition of longstanding practices whereby truckers are paid for fewer hours than they actually work.
"This should allow for significant wage rises," said Michel Caillaud of the National Truckers' Federation.
Truckers say they often work more than 200 hours a month, with many hours unpaid as they wait to load and unload.

Government mediator Robert Cros said Transport Minister Bernard Pons had instructed him to work out a solution on working hours by December 15 and chair a supervisory committee "to ensure what is signed is actually implemented".
The strike in the crucial pre-Christmas commercial period cost European food and haulage industries tens of millions of dollars a day, prompting protests from France's neighbours.
It stranded up to 14,000 Spanish trucks and idled about 90 percent of Portugal's total truck fleet. Belgian ports were clogged by British-bound lorries avoiding France.

The roadblocks have forced some French factories to close down for lack of supplies and cut deliveries of perishable goods ranging from fish to fruit and flowers. In Rouen, in Normandy, 9,000 workers from various sectors were temporarily laid off.
